# Constructing an Interactive Natural Language Interface for Relational Databases

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#nalir)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p73-li.pdf) · PVLDB 8(1), 2014, pages 73-84

**Reading coverage:** All 12 PDF pages: Sections 1-10, definitions, query-tree algorithm, SQL translation examples and Figures 1-13 with captions; no appended supplement.

## Research question

Let non-SQL users verify interpretations of complex database requests rather than trust opaque answer values.

## Method

Maps dependency-tree nodes to schema/data, proposes alternative query trees, inserts inferred implicit nodes under user control and translates the selected tree to SQL. Changing an earlier choice recomputes dependent later interpretations.

## Evaluation

A 14-participant within-subject study on Microsoft Academic Search compares interactive NaLIR, noninteractive NaLIR and website navigation. Tasks are conveyed in Chinese and written as English queries; condition order is fixed.

## What the results support

Interactive users solve 88/98 tasks versus 64/98 without interaction and 56/98 through the website. Four incorrect outputs are still accepted. Candidate-tree coverage limits difficult requests.

## Limits and qualifications

Evidence covers one domain and a small bilingual sample; fixed ordering permits learning effects. Reported time measures only successful tasks. Heuristic implicit-node insertion and top-five interpretations do not guarantee intent correctness.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Establishes interpretation feedback and dependency-aware reprocessing as practical design ideas, while showing residual user verification failures.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The system is broadly reliable and usable. | The single-domain study supports improved task completion, but four wrong answers were accepted and difficult query trees were missing from menus. | Sections 7.2-7.3; Figures 11-13 | Bound to the tested users/tasks; not universal reliability. |
| Interaction time remains practical. | The timing excludes unsuccessful tasks and a three-minute timeout applies. | Sections 7.1-7.3/Figure 13 | Successful-task timing, not full workload latency. |
